source_refs.note: Topic 4.9, printed pages 124-125: glycoproteins, glycolipids, lipoproteins and nucleoproteins.

blocks.text: Conjugated molecules are formed by the combination of two or more molecules belonging to different categories. Some important conjugated molecules are glycoproteins, glycolipids, lipoproteins and nucleoproteins.

blocks.title: Conjugated molecule
blocks.text: A molecule formed by combining two or more molecules from different categories of biomolecule, for example a protein with a carbohydrate, a lipid with a carbohydrate, a lipid with a protein, or a nucleic acid with a protein.

Glycoproteins are formed by a covalent linkage between a protein and a carbohydrate polymer. They occur widely in nature: as integral structural components of membranes, in blood serum, as cellular secretions, and in cartilage, eyes, skin and other tissues.
Glycolipids are formed by a covalent linkage between a lipid and a carbohydrate. They are an integral structural component of membranes.

Lipoproteins are a class of biomolecules formed by hydrophobic interactions, not covalent or ionic bonds, between lipids and proteins. They are the basic structural framework of all types of plasma membrane. Lipids are transported in blood as very low-density lipoproteins.

Nucleoproteins are formed by ionic bonds between chromosomal DNA and proteins. For example, histone proteins bound to DNA form nucleosomes. They stabilise chromosomal structure in eukaryotes and also play an important role in the regulation of gene expression.
